title: Diversity types: neutral, phylogenetic and functional
text: Hill numbers one-parameter family. order q sets much weight rare taxa carry: q = 0 — richness: every taxon counts equally, abundance ignored. q = 1 — Shannon diversity: taxa weighted frequency (exponential Shannon entropy). q = 2 — Simpson diversity: dominated common taxa (inverse Simpson concentration). Hill numbers effective number taxa (“many equally-abundant taxa give diversity”), values across q directly comparable. diversity profile sweeps q continuously — see profiles article.

title: Diversity types: neutral, phylogenetic and functional
text: counts alone get neutral diversity, treats every taxon equally distinct:

title: Diversity types: neutral, phylogenetic and functional
text: Supply phylogenetic tree (class phylo, e.g. ape::read.tree()) whose tip labels match taxa. Diversity measured units branch length, crediting samples span deeper, divergent lineages (Chao et al. 2010). tip labels must cover taxa count table. hilldiv3 reorders counts match tree internally — frequent source silent error older tools — raises informative error name sets disagree. intentionally drop taxa missing one side, align first match_data() (see data-preparation article). q = 0, phylogenetic Hill numbers relate directly Faith’s PD.

title: Diversity types: neutral, phylogenetic and functional
text: Supply dist matrix pairwise functional distances taxa. Diversity accounts trait-different taxa : sample three similar taxa less functionally diverse three contrasting ones (Chiu & Chao 2014).
code: # A toy functional distance matrix over the three taxa. fdist <- as.matrix(dist(   data.frame(body = c(1, 0.2, 0.9), diet = c(0, 1, 1),              row.names = c("t1", "t2", "t3")) )) hilldiv(counts, dist = fdist) #> Computing functional Hill numbers of "q0", "q1", and #> "q2". #>          s1       s2       s3       s4 #> q0 1.601908 2.046926 2.000000 1.946876 #> q1 1.566804 1.739361 1.979626 1.909900 #> q2 1.535588 1.569081 1.960000 1.878525

title: Getting started with hilldiv3
text: hillpart() splits diversity across samples alpha (within-sample), gamma (pooled) beta (gamma / alpha, number effectively distinct communities): hilldiss() hillsim() turn beta bounded dissimilarity / similarity metrics (Sorensen-, Jaccard-, Unifrac-type), hillpair() returns dist object pairwise dissimilarities ready ordination:
code: hillpart(counts) #> Partitioning neutral Hill numbers of "q0", "q1", and #> "q2". #>       alpha    gamma     beta #> q0 2.500000 3.000000 1.200000 #> q1 2.154269 2.905735 1.348827 #> q2 1.968927 2.828374 1.436505 hilldiss(counts, q = 1) #> dissimilarity from neutral Hill numbers of "q1". #>            S         C         U         V #> q1 0.3448199 0.2158525 0.2158525 0.1162756

title: Partitioning and (dis)similarity
text: hillpart() returns three components per diversity order: alpha — effective diversity typical single sample. gamma — effective diversity samples pooled. beta — gamma / alpha, effective number distinct communities. ranges 1 (samples identical) N (samples completely distinct), N number samples. Beta multiplicative decomposition Jost (2007): independent alpha, makes comparable across datasets different richness.
code: hillpart(counts) #> Partitioning neutral Hill numbers of "q0", "q1", and #> "q2". #>       alpha    gamma     beta #> q0 2.500000 3.000000 1.200000 #> q1 2.154269 2.905735 1.348827 #> q2 1.968927 2.828374 1.436505

title: Partitioning and (dis)similarity
text: Beta lives [1, N], awkward compare across studies different sample counts. hilldiss() hillsim() rescale [0, 1] using four overlap measures Chiu et al. (2014): Request single metric order get plain matrix slice: choice q matters much metric: q = 0 weights presence/ absence (turnover rare taxa), q = 2 reflects shifts among dominant taxa.
code: hilldiss(counts)            # dissimilarities, one column per metric #> dissimilarity from neutral Hill numbers of "q0", "q1", #> and "q2". #>            S          C         U          V #> q0 0.2222222 0.06666667 0.2222222 0.06666667 #> q1 0.3448199 0.21585249 0.2158525 0.11627556 #> q2 0.4051548 0.40515478 0.1455017 0.14550174 hillsim(counts)             # similarities = 1 - dissimilarity #> similarity from neutral Hill numbers of "q0", "q1", and #> "q2". #>            S         C         U         V #> q0 0.7777778 0.9333333 0.7777778 0.9333333 #> q1 0.6551801 0.7841475 0.7841475 0.8837244 #> q2 0.5948452 0.5948452 0.8544983 0.8544983 hilldiss(counts, q = 1, metric = "C") #> dissimilarity from neutral Hill numbers of "q1". #> [1] 0.2158525

title: Partitioning and (dis)similarity
text: hilldiss() summarises samples . compare samples two--two — input ordination methods expect — use hillpair(), returns dist object (long tibble): dist drops straight ordination clustering:  Ask several orders/metrics get named list dist objects (e.g. q0S, q1C): tidy long table, convenient ggplot2 dplyr:
code: d <- hillpair(counts, q = 1, metric = "C") #> Computing neutral pairwise dissimilarity for 6 sample pairs. d #>            s1         s2         s3 #> s2 0.52298484                       #> s3 0.47119926 0.08924381            #> s4 0.09902103 0.29281463 0.33948330 pcoa <- cmdscale(d, k = 2) plot(pcoa, type = "n", xlab = "PCoA 1", ylab = "PCoA 2") text(pcoa, labels = rownames(pcoa)) ds <- hillpair(counts, q = c(0, 2), metric = c("C", "U")) #> Computing neutral pairwise dissimilarity for 6 sample pairs. names(ds) #> [1] "q0C" "q2C" "q0U" "q2U" head(hillpair(counts, q = 1, metric = "C", out = "tibble")) #> Computing neutral pairwise dissimilarity for 6 sample pairs. #>   first second q metric      value #> 1    s1     s2 1      C 0.52298484 #> 2    s1     s3 1      C 0.47119926 #> 3    s1     s4 1      C 0.09902103 #> 4    s2     s3 1      C 0.08924381 #> 5    s2     s4 1      C 0.29281463 #> 6    s3     s4 1      C 0.33948330

title: Preparing your data
text: can pass following — coerced internally representation, call functions way: numeric matrix (taxa × samples); data frame tibble counts taxa row names; numeric vector single sample (names taxa); phyloseq object — OTU table read, transposed needed, embedded phylogeny picked automatically; TreeSummarizedExperiment — assay used counts rowTree phylogeny. pass phyloseq TreeSummarizedExperiment already carries tree, phylogenetic diversity works without supplying tree :
code: # A single sample as a named vector. hilldiv(c(t1 = 10, t2 = 2, t3 = 3)) #> Computing neutral Hill numbers of "q0", "q1", and #> "q2". #>     sample1 #> q0 3.000000 #> q1 2.365174 #> q2 1.991150 library(phyloseq) ps <- phyloseq(   otu_table(counts, taxa_are_rows = TRUE),   phy_tree(ape::read.tree(text = "((t1:1,t2:1):1,t3:2);")) ) hilldiv(ps)        # phylogenetic, tree taken from the object #> Computing phylogenetic Hill numbers of "q0", "q1", and #> "q2". #>     s1       s2       s3       s4 #> q0 1.5 2.000000 1.500000 2.000000 #> q1 1.5 1.598520 1.406992 1.677678 #> q2 1.5 1.406977 1.324324 1.500000

what: Matching counts to a tree or distances
title: Preparing your data
text: Phylogenetic functional analyses require taxa count table line tree tips distance-matrix names. hilldiv3 enforces one place: checks two name sets setequal() (order matter); reorders counts match reference — eliminating silent misalignment plagued earlier tools; sets disagree, stops message listing offending taxa.
code: bad_tree <- ape::read.tree(text = "((t1:1,t2:1):1,t9:2);") hilldiv(counts, tree = bad_tree) #> Error in `.abort_mismatch()`: #> ! Taxa names in the count data and the tree tips do not match. #> ℹ Only in counts: "t3" #> ℹ Only in tree tips: "t9"

previous_headings: Matching counts to a tree or distances
title: Preparing your data
text: Real datasets rarely match perfectly — reference tree may include taxa never observed, table may carry taxa absent tree. match_data() restricts reorders count table shared taxa, reporting dropped, can curate alignment analysis: Feed aligned table back — now name sets agree analysis runs: match_data() works way dist argument functional data.
code: tree <- ape::read.tree(text = "((t1:1,t2:1):1,t4:2);")   # has t4, lacks t3 matched <- match_data(counts, tree = tree) #> Dropped 1 taxon from `data` not in the tree tips. #> 1 taxon in the tree tips has no counts; prune it before downstream analysis. matched #>    s1 s2 s3 s4 #> t1 10  2  3  6 #> t2  0  8  4  2 tree3 <- ape::read.tree(text = "(t1:1,t2:1);") hilldiv(match_data(counts, tree = tree3), tree = tree3) #> Dropped 1 taxon from `data` not in the tree tips. #> Computing phylogenetic Hill numbers of "q0", "q1", and "q2". #>    s1       s2       s3       s4 #> q0  1 2.000000 2.000000 2.000000 #> q1  1 1.649385 1.979626 1.754765 #> q2  1 1.470588 1.960000 1.600000

title: Preparing your data
text: Putting together:
code: # 1. Counts + traits in hand. traits <- data.frame(   body_mass = c(1.0, 0.2, 0.9),   diet      = factor(c("herb", "carn", "carn")),   row.names = c("t1", "t2", "t3") )  # 2. Derive a functional distance matrix. fdist <- traits2dist(traits)  # 3. Align counts to it (here they already match). counts2 <- match_data(counts, dist = fdist)  # 4. Measure and compare. hilldiv(counts2, dist = fdist) #> Computing functional Hill numbers of "q0", "q1", and #> "q2". #>          s1       s2       s3       s4 #> q0 1.353846 1.911682 2.000000 1.650074 #> q1 1.343253 1.658248 1.979626 1.617041 #> q2 1.333333 1.517241 1.960000 1.590106 hilldiss(counts2, dist = fdist, q = 1) #> dissimilarity from functional Hill numbers of "q1". #>            S         C         U          V #> q1 0.1629541 0.0940307 0.0940307 0.04641062

title: Profiles, evenness and redundancy
text: single q can mislead: two samples can identical richness different Shannon Simpson diversity, ranking can even flip q increases. profile plots Hill numbers across continuous sweep q, making full picture visible. hillprof() evaluates fine grid orders (0 3 default): result tidy long-format object ready-made plot method — one declining curve per sample:  read : height q = 0 richness; height q → ∞ reflects dominance. flat curve means even community (diversity barely changes q); steep curve means taxa dominate. two curves cross, neither sample unambiguously diverse — answer depends much weight rare taxa. Profiles work phylogenetic functional diversity , can grab matrix instead tidy form:
code: prof <- hillprof(counts) #> Computing neutral diversity profile over 31 orders. head(prof) #>     q sample    value #> 1 0.0     s1 2.000000 #> 2 0.1     s1 1.988282 #> 3 0.2     s1 1.976692 #> 4 0.3     s1 1.965243 #> 5 0.4     s1 1.953945 #> 6 0.5     s1 1.942809 plot(prof) phylo_prof <- hillprof(counts, tree = tree) #> Computing phylogenetic diversity profile over 31 orders. mat <- hillprof(counts, out = "matrix") #> Computing neutral diversity profile over 31 orders. mat[1:3, ] #>            s1       s2       s3       s4 #> q0   2.000000 3.000000 2.000000 3.000000 #> q0.1 1.988282 2.889634 1.997940 2.961206 #> q0.2 1.976692 2.783926 1.995884 2.924319

title: Profiles, evenness and redundancy
text: Evenness asks equitably abundance distributed, independent richness. hilleven() expresses ratio diversity order q richness (qD / 0D), bounded [0, 1]: 1 perfectly even, lower values mean stronger dominance. exactly normalised height diversity profile — single sample’s profile flatness summarised number. Reading column tells dominated sample ; s2 least even.

title: Profiles, evenness and redundancy
text: Neutral diversity counts taxa; phylogenetic functional diversity count distinct lineages trait combinations. taxa closely related functionally similar, much neutral diversity redundant — losing taxon costs little unique phylogenetic/functional diversity. hillred() quantifies fitting saturating relationship neutral diversity (x) phylogenetic/functional diversity (y) across samples, y = -· 2^(-x / b) + c, summarising redundancy 1 - b / max(x). therefore needs tree dist, several samples fit curve: returned matrix redundancy summary plus fitted , b, c coefficients per order. Values near 1 mean assemblage highly redundant (taxa phylogenetically/functionally interchangeable); values near 0 mean taxon contributes largely unique diversity. Note. Redundancy curve fit across samples can fail converge orders small degenerate datasets, case row NA warning explains . Fit real datasets enough samples spanning range neutral diversity.
code: hillred(counts, tree = tree) #> Warning: Redundancy for "q0" could not be estimated: singular gradient matrix at initial #> parameter estimates #> Warning: Redundancy for "q2" could not be estimated: step factor 0.000488281 reduced #> below 'minFactor' of 0.000976562 #>    redundancy        a         b        c #> q0         NA       NA        NA       NA #> q1  0.8050446 4.223956 0.5251091 1.803386 #> q2         NA       NA        NA       NA

text: Tools analysing diversity biological communities (e.g. OTU/ASV/MAG tables) based Hill numbers.
